title: Polyclonal breast milk–derived secretory IgA confers broad antiviral protection against multiple respiratory viruses
abstract: Passive immunization is an important tool for protecting individuals with primary immune deficiencies from infectious diseases and offers a rapid response strategy for protecting vulnerable populations, particularly during the interval between pathogen emergence and vaccine deployment. Current approaches rely on intravenous delivery of IgG-enriched plasma or monoclonal antibodies, which limits accessibility, scalability, and effectiveness at mucosal surfaces, the primary entry point for respiratory viruses. Here, we tested LCTG-001, a polyclonal secretory IgA preparation derived from pooled human breast milk, to address these limitations. LCTG-001 demonstrated broad antiviral activity against clinically relevant respiratory viruses, including respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, and influenza A virus. LCTG-001 effectively recognized both group 1 and group 2 influenza A subtypes, including the highly pathogenic H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b, and engaged nonneutralizing effector mechanisms such as neuraminidase inhibition and neutrophil activation. When administered intranasally, LCTG-001 conferred complete protection against influenza A challenge in both immunocompetent and antibody-deficient murine models, preventing morbidity and mortality through a transient early reduction in viral burden followed by sustained improvements in lung pathology and lung barrier integrity. These findings highlight the potential of breast milk–derived secretory IgA as a scalable, mucosa-targeted passive immunization strategy capable of addressing both endemic and emerging respiratory viral threats.

title: The transition to postpartum lactation establishes a state of maternal antiviral resilience
abstract: Influenza A virus (IAV) causes severe disease during late pregnancy, yet how maternal adaptations in host defense shape susceptibility following childbirth remains unknown. Here, we show that the postpartum period represents a state of enhanced maternal antiviral immunity. Across postpartum stages, dams infected before weaning exhibited increased survival and reduced disease following lethal IAV challenge compared with nonpregnant females. Postpartum protection was associated with enhanced viral clearance and increased pulmonary antigen-specific CD8+ T cells and IL-17A-producing gamma-delta T cells. We identify the transition into lactation as a critical determinant of this protection. Protection extended to highly pathogenic avian influenza. Together, these findings reveal that maternal antiviral immunity remains actively shaped after childbirth, establishing the postpartum lactational period as a distinct state of maternal antiviral resilience.

title: Pre-existing systemic and nasal antibodies against avian H5 influenza A viruses vary according to childhood imprinting
abstract: ABSTRACT Avian influenza A viruses (IAVs) pose a constant pandemic threat, with the recent 2.3.4.4b clade of the H5 subtype causing high pathogenicity and spreading across animal species and geographic locations. Understanding human pre-existing immunity to avian H5 IAV can inform on population susceptibility, a critical aspect of pandemic preparedness. To that end, we analyzed the IAV HA-specific antibodies across individuals born between 1928 and 1999 with different early life exposures to IAV subtypes. Individuals born prior to 1957 had the highest pre-existing serum antibodies to group 1 HA antigens, including the 2.3.4.4b H5 and a group 1 HA stem antigen. These birth year-specific patterns were not reflected in the limited pre-existing serum neutralizing antibodies detectable against a 2.3.4.4b H5 IAV or in H5-specific memory B cell populations. They were, however, evident in pre-existing nasal IgG and IgA titers to H5, which were greater in individuals born prior to 1957. Our findings demonstrate that the immunological biases afforded by early life exposure extend to antibodies detected in the nasal mucosa, the site of IAV replication. IMPORTANCE Understating pre-existing immunity to influenza A viruses (IAVs) of pandemic potential is an important aspect of pandemic preparedness. This includes an understanding of the heterogeneity of pre-existing immunity across the population. Here, we demonstrate that pre-existing antibodies to H5 IAV vary according to the year of birth and childhood imprinting. We demonstrate that this is the case for both systemic and nasal antibodies, highlighting the importance of understanding pre-existing mucosal immunity at the sites of influenza virus replication.

title: BIOSECURITY IN PIG FARMS
abstract: Pig farming is an important source of livelihood, animal protein and income for smallholder, tribal and commercial farmers in India, particularly in the North-Eastern states. The sector is repeatedly threatened by transboundary and endemic diseases such as African swine fever (ASF), classical swine fever (CSF), porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome (PRRS), foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) and porcine epidemic diarrhoea (PED). Several pig-associated pathogens, including swine influenza viruses, Japanese encephalitis virus, Streptococcus suis and Taenia solium, are also of public health importance. In the absence of a commercial vaccine for ASF, biosecurity remains the most effective and economical tool to prevent, control and contain pig diseases. Biosecurity comprises external measures (bioexclusion), which prevent the entry of pathogens into a farm, and internal measures (biocontainment and biomanagement), which limit pathogen spread within and out of a farm. This review describes the concept and principles of biosecurity, the major diseases and transmission routes relevant to pig farms, practical external and internal biosecurity measures, cleaning and disinfection protocols, and tools for biosecurity assessment such as Biocheck.UGent. It also discusses the economic benefits of biosecurity, its role in reducing antimicrobial use under a One Health approach, and the specific constraints of smallholder and backyard pig systems in India following the incursion of ASF in 2020. Strengthened farmer training, regulated pig movement, swill-feeding control, compartmentalisation and institutional support are recommended to improve biosecurity compliance in Indian pig production.

title: Breaking the channel barrier: same-fluorescence, different-Tm probe strategy enables seven-target respiratory virus detection on a six-channel PCR platform within 20 minutes.
abstract: BACKGROUND Respiratory pathogens with overlapping symptoms-including SARS-CoV-2, influenza A/B, H5/H7/H10 avian influenza, and RSV-co-circulate and co-infect, demanding rapid multiplex screening at points of care. Conventional multiplex real-time PCR is constrained by hardware channel capacity (≤6), making it difficult to detect seven targets while distinguishing influenza A and B in a single tube. This work addresses the contradiction between high-order multiplexing and limited fluorescence channels without sacrificing speed or sensitivity. RESULTS We developed a six-channel ultra-fast PCR platform detecting seven respiratory viruses in a single tube within 20 min, using a same-fluorescence, different-Tm probe strategy. Influenza A and B share the FAM channel yet generate distinct melting peaks (∼12 °C difference, 84.8 °C vs. 72.3 °C), enabling accurate typing via melting curve analysis. Primers, probes, and enzymes are pre-embedded as lyophilized beads in sealed cartridges for fully automated sample-to-result operation. The assay achieved 100% detection at 5 copies/test for all targets, linearity (R2 > 0.95) across 5-105 copies/test, 90-110% efficiencies, and no cross-reactivity against 39 non-target pathogens. Cartridges remained stable for 12 months at 25 °C. Validation on 271 clinical specimens showed 100% agreement with sequencing-verified single-plex qPCR. SIGNIFICANCE AND NOVELTY This work provides the first integration of melting-curve-based same-channel multiplexing with lyophilized cartridge technology on an ultra-fast PCR platform. By overcoming channel limitations while maintaining speed and sensitivity, the system offers a practical, field-deployable screening tool for decentralized respiratory pathogen detection in resource-limited settings.

full_text: Abstract Purpose of Review Highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) has moved from recurrent poultry epizootics to a geographically extensive, multi-host panzootic involving wild birds, domestic animals, marine and terrestrial mammals, and exposed people. This expert review examines the epidemiologic transitions that produced the present wildlife-livestock-human interface and identifies surveillance priorities supported by original epidemiologic, genomic, experimental, and environmental studies. Recent Findings Recent primary studies show that clade 2.3.4.4b viruses are repeatedly introduced and redistributed by wild birds, can reach remote ecosystems, and have generated consequential mammalian outbreaks. The dairy-cattle emergence was especially important because genomic and pathology data demonstrated mammary-gland tropism, efficient cattle-to-cattle spread, interstate dissemination through animal movement, and secondary exposure of farm workers. Environmental sampling of water and sediment can complement bird sampling, while paired serology can complement investigation of confirmed occupational infections. full_text_sections.full_text: Abstract Purpose of Review Highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) has moved from recurrent poultry epizootics to a geographically extensive, multi-host panzootic involving wild birds, domestic animals, marine and terrestrial mammals, and exposed people. This expert review examines the epidemiologic transitions that produced the present wildlife-livestock-human interface and identifies surveillance priorities supported by original epidemiologic, genomic, experimental, and environmental studies. Recent Findings Recent primary studies show that clade 2.3.4.4b viruses are repeatedly introduced and redistributed by wild birds, can reach remote ecosystems, and have generated consequential mammalian outbreaks. The dairy-cattle emergence was especially important because genomic and pathology data demonstrated mammary-gland tropism, efficient cattle-to-cattle spread, interstate dissemination through animal movement, and secondary exposure of farm workers. Environmental sampling of water and sediment can complement bird sampling, while paired serology can complement investigation of confirmed occupational infections. Summary Surveillance should shift from separate poultry, wildlife, livestock, and human programs toward risk-based One Health networks that link field observations, laboratory testing, genomic data, animal movements, environmental matrices, and occupational health. Priority outcomes are earlier detection, faster cross-sector investigation, and rapid recognition of viral changes associated with altered host range or transmission. title_original: Wildlife-Livestock-Human Interfaces in the Global H5N1 Panzootic: Epidemiologic Shifts and Surveillance Priorities

analysis.scope_and_question: Avian influenza A viruses, avian-origin zoonotic infections, and qualified avian subtypes. The review focuses on the epidemiologic shifts of H5N1 and other avian influenza viruses from poultry epizootics to a panzootic involving wild birds, domestic animals, and humans. The central question is how these viruses have transitioned across species and environments, and what surveillance strategies are needed.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is an expert analysis of original epidemiologic, genomic, experimental, and environmental studies. It does not report on study counts, databases, or meta-analysis. The methods section includes a case-control study of risk factors for avian influenza A (H5N1) disease in Hong Kong, 1997, and references to primary studies on clade 2.3.4.4b viruses. The review does not describe a formal meta-analysis or consensus process.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review concludes that H5N1 viruses have transitioned from poultry epizootics to a panzootic involving multiple hosts, including wild birds, domestic animals, and humans. It highlights the importance of clade 2.3.4.4b viruses in this transition, noting their ability to reach remote ecosystems and cause consequential mammalian outbreaks. The dairy-cattle emergence is emphasized due to its implications for transmission and zoonotic potential.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review identifies gaps in understanding the mechanisms of cross-species transmission and the environmental factors that facilitate viral spread. It notes that while genomic and pathology data support the role of H5N1 in mammalian outbreaks, there is limited evidence on the full extent of its host range and the specific pathways of transmission to humans. The review also highlights the need for more comprehensive surveillance across wildlife-livestock-human interfaces.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review recommends shifting surveillance efforts toward risk-based One Health networks that integrate field observations, laboratory testing, genomic data, animal movements, and occupational health. It emphasizes the importance of early detection, faster cross-sector investigation, and rapid recognition of viral changes associated with altered host range or transmission. Environmental sampling and paired serology are suggested as complementary tools for monitoring H5N1 activity.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores the epidemiologic shifts of avian influenza A(H5N1) viruses from poultry epizootics to a panzootic involving wild birds, domestic animals, and humans. It highlights the role of clade 2.3.4.4b viruses in spreading to remote ecosystems and causing mammalian outbreaks, particularly in dairy cattle. The review underscores the need for integrated surveillance strategies that combine field observations, genomic data, and environmental sampling. It identifies gaps in understanding transmission mechanisms and calls for improved cross-sector collaboration to detect and respond to viral changes. The implications emphasize the importance of risk-based One Health networks for monitoring and mitigating the spread of H5N1.

elements_zh.scope_and_question: 禽流感 A 病毒、禽源性人兽共患病和合格的禽亚型。本回顾重点研究了H5N1和其他禽流感病毒从家禽流行病转变为涉及野生动物、家养动物和人类的泛流行病的流行病学转变。中心问题是这些病毒如何跨越物种和环境进行传播,以及需要哪些监测策略。
elements_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 本回顾是对原始流行病学、基因组、实验和环境研究的专家分析。它没有报告研究数量、数据库或元分析。方法部分包括了1997年香港禽流感 A (H5N1) 疾病风险因素的队列研究,以及关于clade 2.3.4.4b 病毒的初步研究参考。本回顾没有描述正式的元分析或共识过程。
elements_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 本回顾得出结论,H5N1 病毒已从家禽流行病转变为涉及多种宿主的泛流行病,包括野生动物、家养动物和人类。它强调了clade 2.3.4.4b 病毒在这一转变中的重要性,指出它们能够到达偏远生态系统并引起重要的哺乳动物暴发。特别强调了奶牛的出现,因为它对传播和人兽共患病的潜在影响。
elements_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 本回顾指出了对跨物种传播机制和促进病毒传播的环境因素的理解不足。它指出,虽然基因组和病理数据支持H5N1在哺乳动物暴发中的作用,但对其全面的宿主范围和向人类传播的具体途径的证据有限。本回顾还强调了需要更全面的监测以监测野生动物-家畜-人类界面。
elements_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 本回顾建议将监测努力转向基于风险的一体化健康网络,该网络整合了现场观察、实验室测试、基因组数据、动物移动和职业健康。它强调了早期检测、跨部门调查的快速性以及对与宿主范围或传播相关的病毒变化的快速识别的重要性。环境采样和配对的血清学被建议作为监测H5N1活动的补充工具。

analysis_en.scope_and_question: Avian influenza A viruses, avian-origin zoonotic infections, and qualified avian subtypes. The review focuses on the epidemiologic shifts of H5N1 and other avian influenza viruses from poultry epizootics to a panzootic involving wild birds, domestic animals, and humans. The central question is how these viruses have transitioned across species and environments, and what surveillance strategies are needed.
analysis_en.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is an expert analysis of original epidemiologic, genomic, experimental, and environmental studies. It does not report on study counts, databases, or meta-analysis. The methods section includes a case-control study of risk factors for avian influenza A (H5N1) disease in Hong Kong, 1997, and references to primary studies on clade 2.3.4.4b viruses. The review does not describe a formal meta-analysis or consensus process.
analysis_en.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review concludes that H5N1 viruses have transitioned from poultry epizootics to a panzootic involving multiple hosts, including wild birds, domestic animals, and humans. It highlights the importance of clade 2.3.4.4b viruses in this transition, noting their ability to reach remote ecosystems and cause consequential mammalian outbreaks. The dairy-cattle emergence is emphasized due to its implications for transmission and zoonotic potential.
analysis_en.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review identifies gaps in understanding the mechanisms of cross-species transmission and the environmental factors that facilitate viral spread. It notes that while genomic and pathology data support the role of H5N1 in mammalian outbreaks, there is limited evidence on the full extent of its host range and the specific pathways of transmission to humans. The review also highlights the need for more comprehensive surveillance across wildlife-livestock-human interfaces.
analysis_en.research_and_practice_implications: The review recommends shifting surveillance efforts toward risk-based One Health networks that integrate field observations, laboratory testing, genomic data, animal movements, and occupational health. It emphasizes the importance of early detection, faster cross-sector investigation, and rapid recognition of viral changes associated with altered host range or transmission. Environmental sampling and paired serology are suggested as complementary tools for monitoring H5N1 activity.

This expert review examines the epidemiologic transitions that produced the present wildlife-livestock-human interface and identifies surveillance priorities supported by original epidemiologic, genomic, experimental, and environmental studies. Recent Findings Recent primary studies show that clade 2.3.4.4b viruses are repeatedly introduced and redistributed by wild birds, can reach remote ecosystems, and have generated consequential mammalian outbreaks. No software code, computational model, or analytical algorithm was developed for this review. This review did not generate or use new biological materials, experimental resources, or proprietary datasets. Case-control study of risk factors for avian influenza A (H5N1) disease, Hong Kong, 1997. The dairy-cattle emergence was especially important because genomic and pathology data demonstrated mammary-gland tropism, efficient cattle-to-cattle spread, interstate dissemination through animal movement, and secondary exposure of farm workers. full_text: IntroductionHighly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b has spread widely across South America, but its genomic diversity and patterns of introduction into Ecuador remain poorly characterized.MethodsIn this study, we report and characterize four genomes of A(H5N1) viruses detected in four individuals of two Ecuadorian seabird species: two magnificent frigatebirds (Fregata magnificens) and two blue-footed boobies (Sula nebouxii) sampled in 2023.ResultsThese genomes represent confirmed detections of avian influenza in wild birds in the country. The viruses were assigned to genotype B3.2. Global phylogenetic analysis showed that the Ecuadorian wild-bird viruses formed groups distinct from viruses detected in domestic birds in Ecuador. Subsequent phylogenetic and phylogeographic analyses within the South American dataset placed our samples in two distinct clusters, each closely related to viruses previously detected in Peru. These findings highlight the genetic diversity of genotype B3.2 viruses detected in Ecuador and their relationship to viruses circulating in the region. FluServer screening identified 29 amino acid substitutions previously associated with virulence, antigenic change, host specificity, polymerase activity, or antiviral resistance.DiscussionThese findings provide genomic evidence of repeated H5N1 introductions into Ecuador as part of the regional spread of the virus along the eastern Pacific coast. They also support sustained surveillance across wildlife, animal-health, and public-health sectors. 2Materials and methods2.1Sample collectionTracheal swab samples were collected from four individuals of two seabird species in Ecuador: two frigatebirds (F. magnificens), one sick and one found dead, sampled in San Vicente, Manabí Province in January 2023; and two sick blue-footed boobies (S. nebouxii) sampled in General Villamil Playas, Guayas Province in May 2023 (Figures 1A–C). Sampling was conducted by the Ministry of Environment and Energy (Ministerio de Ambiente y Energía) (Supplementary material 1).Figure 1(A) Frigatebird (Fregata magnificens) sample collection: tracheal swab. (B) Blue-footed booby (Sula nebouxii) sample collection: tracheal swab. (C) Map of Ecuador showing collection points: San Vicente-Manabí and Villamil Playas-Guayas.Panel A shows individuals in blue protective suits handling a large black bird with a red throat pouch, while the adjacent image shows close-up handling of the bird’s foot, Frigatebird. Panel B displays a seabird with blue feet standing on rocks, followed by gloved hands collecting a sample from the bird’s beak, Blue-footed booby. Panel C is a color-coded map of Ecuador, including the Galapagos Islands, with two marked locations on the Pacific Coast indicating sampling sites in Manabí and Santa Elena, and a legend categorizing regions by Pacific Coast, Andes, Amazon basin, and Galapagos.2.2Diagnostic confirmation, genotyping, and whole-genome sequencingTracheal swab samples were initially tested for influenza A(H5N1) virus by RT-qPCR at LABIGEN, a private laboratory located in Quito. Diagnostic confirmation and genotyping were subsequently performed at the INSPI, Quito headquarters. Samples were confirmed as positive for influenza A(H5) virus by RT-qPCR at the Zonal Laboratory for Influenza and Other Respiratory Viruses. Whole-genome sequencing and bioinformatic analyses were conducted at the National Reference Center for Genomics, Sequencing and Bioinformatics (Centro de Referencia Nacional de Genómica, Secuenciación y Bioinformática, CRN-GENSBIO). Sequencing was performed on an Illumina MiSeq instrument using the Illumina Respiratory Virus Oligo Panel (RVOP) and a MiSeq v2 150-cycle reagent kit (Illumina, Inc., n.d.). The quality of the FASTQ files was evaluated using FastQC (Andrews, 2010), and adapter sequences and low-quality bases were removed using Trimmomatic (Bolger et al., 2014). Filtered reads were mapped using Bowtie2 v2.5.1 (Langmead and Salzberg, 2012) against the eight genomic segments of the influenza A/goose/Guangdong/1/1996 (H5N1) reference virus: PB2 (NC_007357.1), PB1 (NC_007358.1), PA (NC_007359.1), HA (NC_007362.1), NP (NC_007360.1), NA (NC_007361.1), M (NC_007363.1), and NS (NC_007364.1). Consensus sequences were generated from the mapped reads. Four whole-genome sequences, one from each sampled bird, were obtained and deposited in GISAID under accession numbers EPI_ISL_17973443, EPI_ISL_17973458, EPI_ISL_18137626, and EPI_ISL_18137671.2.3Neuraminidase subtype, clade, and genotype assignmentThe neuraminidase subtype was determined by sequence similarity searches using the Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (BLAST) and the Bacterial and Viral Bioinformatics Resource Center (BV-BRC) (Altschul et al., 1990; Olson et al., 2023). Clade assignment was based on phylogenetic analysis of the HA segment. The HA sequences of the Ecuadorian viruses were analyzed together with a reference dataset of 625 avian influenza A(H5) virus sequences retrieved from BV-BRC. This analysis classified the four Ecuadorian viruses as highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) viruses belonging to clade 2.3.4.4b.Genotype assignment was conducted using GenoFLU v1.01, which utilizes BLAST to identify each genome segment against a curated reference database and assigns genotypes according to the resulting eight-segment constellation (Youk et al., 2023a). Genotypes were assigned based on similarity calculations.2.4Exploratory phylogenetic reconstruction using augurAn exploratory phylogenetic analysis was conducted using the Augur bioinformatics pipeline implemented in Nextstrain version 24.3.0 (Huddleston et al., 2021). The dataset included all available highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) virus sequences deposited in the GISAID database up to 9 September 2026 that corresponded to clade 2.3.4.4b and had been assigned to genotype B3.2.The analysis was performed using nucleotide sequences from the hemagglutinin (HA) segment. Sequences were filtered to retain only those with at least 90% coverage of the segment. Sequences were excluded if they lacked complete collection-date or sampling-location information, had an embargo status in GISAID, or were flagged as having a “type mismatch,” indicating an inconsistency between the submitted sequence and its associated virus metadata. Following the application of these filters, 2,314 sequences were retained for the exploratory analysis. These sequences contained both sampling-location and collection-date information suitable for phylogenetic and temporal analyses.The main parameters used throughout the Augur workflow are described below, including those applied during sequence alignment, phylogenetic inference, temporal reconstruction, and visualization. Nucleotide sequences were aligned using MAFFT v7 (Katoh and Standley, 2013). A maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tree was inferred using IQ-TREE v2.2.0 (Minh et al., 2020) under the general time-reversible (GTR) nucleotide substitution model, selected using ModelFinder. Nodal support was assessed using 1,000 bootstrap replicates. The resulting maximum-likelihood topology was converted into a time-scaled phylogeny using TreeTime version 0.11.4 (Sagulenko et al., 2018). Temporal calibration incorporated the sampling dates of the sequences and a fixed evolutionary rate of 0.008 substitutions per site per year. Internal node dates were estimated using marginal inference to reconstruct the temporal emergence and diversification patterns of genotype B3.2 within H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b. The resulting time-scaled phylogeny, together with the associated geographic metadata and inferred spatiotemporal patterns, was visualized using Auspice. The phylogenetic tree was visualized in RStudio Team (2024).2.5Molecular clock and ancestral state reconstructionAfter completing the exploratory analysis described above, we conducted a more focused analysis by selecting South American sequences that clustered with the Ecuadorian wild-bird sequences reported in this study. The resulting dataset included available sequences from Ecuador, Peru, Chile, Argentina, Uruguay, and other South American countries. We included sequence A/fox/Minnesota/22/016487/001/original/2022 (EPI_ISL_15078249), assigned to genotype B3.2, as a representative sequence for comparison with the South American viruses. Sequences corresponding to the eight influenza A virus genome segments were aligned independently using MAFFT v7 (Katoh and Standley, 2013). The segment-specific alignments were then concatenated to generate a whole-genome alignment. A maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tree was reconstructed using IQ-TREE v2.2.0 (Minh et al., 2020), and the best-fitting nucleotide substitution model was selected with ModelFinder based on the Bayesian information criterion (Kalyaanamoorthy et al., 2017).The temporal signal of the concatenated dataset was assessed through root-to-tip regression using the maximum-likelihood tree as input in TempEst v1.5.3 (Rambaut et al., 2016). The analysis was conducted using both the selected outgroup root and the best-fitting root identified by TempEst. In both rooting schemes, the regression showed a positive relationship between genetic divergence and sampling time, supporting the use of a molecular-clock model. Bayesian phylogenetic reconstruction was performed using BEAST v1.10.5 (Suchard et al., 2018). To account for variation in evolutionary rates among lineages, an uncorrelated lognormal relaxed molecular clock was used. The analysis incorporated a Bayesian Skygrid coalescent model (Gill et al., 2013) and the GTR + F + G4 nucleotide substitution model, which was selected by ModelFinder. Base frequencies were estimated from the alignment, and among-site rate heterogeneity was modeled using four gamma categories. Sampling dates were assigned to the tips.The mean evolutionary rate was assigned a lognormal prior with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.0 on the log scale. The standard deviation of the uncorrelated relaxed-clock rates was assigned an exponential prior with a mean of 1.0. The Skygrid population-size parameters were assigned a 1/x prior. Country was included as discrete traits for ancestral-state and phylogeographic reconstruction following the framework proposed by Lemey et al. (2009). The Markov chain Monte Carlo analysis was run for 100 million generations, with parameters and trees sampled every 10,000 generations. The first 10% of samples were discarded as burn-in. Convergence and mixing were evaluated in Tracer v1.7.2 by inspecting trace plots and confirming effective sample size values greater than 200 for all relevant parameters. A maximum clade credibility tree was summarized using TreeAnnotator v1.1.10.5 and visualized in FigTree v1.4.4 (Rambaut, 2018).2.6Mutations analysisSNPs and mutation analyses were performed to identify amino acid changes with potential biological effects related to virulence, immune escape, host specificity, and drug resistance. Each segment was analyzed using FluSurver1 and compared to the reference influenza genome previously detailed. Only mutations with previously characterized significant biological effects were included in the mutation list. 3Results3.1Genome metricsGenome recovery metrics for the four influenza A(H5N1) genomes are summarized in Table 1. High-depth sequencing data were obtained for all samples, with an average depth of approximately 1,000× in the recovered viral segments. This level of read support allowed for the generation of nearly complete consensus genomes for all viruses, although this varied depending on the segment and sample. Overall segment coverage ranged from 80.0 to 100.0%.Table 1Recovery metrics for influenza A virus genome segments in sequencing samples.SegmentLength (bp)Mean depth (×)Sample 1 coverage (%)Sample 2 coverage (%)Sample 3 coverage (%)Sample 4 coverage (%)PB22,3401,00099.5100.092.585.6PB12,3411,00098.399.390.383.3PA2,2331,00099.299.199.098.7HA1,7511,00099.590.599.780.0NP1,5651,000100.099.698.899.6NA1,4581,00098.590.399.098.1MP1,0271,00099.799.4100.0100.0NS8901,00094.890.9—81.3Sample identification: Sample 1, Fregata magnificens (EPI_ISL_17973443); Sample 2, Fregata magnificens (EPI_ISL_17973458); Sample 3, Sula nebouxii (EPI_ISL_18137626); and Sample 4, Sula nebouxii (EPI_ISL_18137671).Mean sequencing depth was 1,000 × for all segments. An em dash (—) indicates that coverage was not available or could not be calculated.The virus detected in the two F. magnificens specimens showed consistently high recovery across all eight genomic segments, whereas greater variation in coverage was observed in the viruses obtained from the two S. nebouxii specimens. The main limitation was the failure to recover the NS segment from sample 3. Additionally, sample 4 showed lower coverage for some segments, particularly HA. Nevertheless, the recovered sequence data met the predefined quality criteria and provided sufficient genome completeness to support phylogenetic, genotypic, and mutation analyses. The resulting influenza A(H5N1) genomes were deposited in GISAID under accession numbers EPI_ISL_17973443 for sample 1 (F. magnificens), EPI_ISL_17973458 for sample 2 (F. magnificens), EPI_ISL_18137626 for sample 3 (S. nebouxii), and EPI_ISL_18137671 for sample 4 (S. nebouxii).3.2Clade and genotype assignmentPhylogenetic analysis of the hemagglutinin (HA) gene placed all four influenza A(H5N1) viruses detected in Ecuador’s seabirds within clade 2.3.4.4b of the highly pathogenic avian influenza H5 lineage (Figure 2). The sequences detected in Ecuador grouped within the 2.3.4.4b cluster and were phylogenetically distinct from the other clades represented in the analysis, including 2.3.4.4a, 2.3.4.4c, 2.3.4.4d, 2.3.4.4e, 2.3.4.4f, 2.3.4.4g, and 2.3.4.4h. This clustering supported a consistent HA clade assignment for viruses detected in both F. magnificens and S. nebouxii.Figure 2Phylogenetic tree of the hemagglutinin (HA) segment of avian influenza A(H5) viruses. Clade 2.3.4.4b assignment is highlighted in light green. Samples from Ecuador are indicated with light green branch lines.Circular phylogenetic tree diagram showing relationships among various samples with distinct color-coded segments corresponding to ranges labeled 2.3.4.4a through 2.3.4.4b and others. Red dots mark specific branch points, and a tree scale bar is present at the top left. A legend identifies segment colors and their associated groups.Whole-genome genotype assignment was performed using GenoFLU based on the segment-group classification of the eight influenza A virus gene segments. Genome constellations were reported in the order PB2|PB1|PA|HA|NP|NA|M|NS. Samples 1, 2, and 4 showed the same complete segment-group constellation, am2.1|am1.2|ea1|ea1|am1.4.1|ea1|ea1|am1.1, corresponding to genotype B3.2 (Table 2). For Sample 3, the NS segment was not recovered; therefore, the NS segment group could not be assigned. Its genotype classification was reported only based on the seven available segments. No differences in genome constellation were observed between viruses obtained from F. magnificens collected in January 2023 and S. nebouxii collected in May 2023. The tree was reconstructed from hemagglutinin sequences and includes 2,314 sequences retained after applying the quality and metadata filters. For visualization purposes, only 690 sequences are displayed in the tree; the remaining sequences were omitted from the figure to improve readability. Ecuador is represented in the clade labels CHL–ECU–PER and COL–CAN–ECU–O.C.A.–USA, indicating phylogenetic groupings containing sequences from Ecuador and the corresponding countries or geographic regions. full_text_sections.discussion: 4DiscussionThis study presents the genomic characterization of highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b viruses detected in frigatebirds (F. magnificens) and blue-footed boobies (S. nebouxii) from coastal Ecuador during the early phase of the South American epizootic. These cases represent confirmed detections of avian influenza in wild birds in Ecuador. Although all four viruses shared the B3.2 genome constellation, they were distributed into two temporally and phylogenetically distinct clusters, both closely related to viruses detected in Peru. This pattern indicates genetic heterogeneity among the Ecuadorian wild seabird viruses and is compatible with independent introduction events; however, the available data do not allow the number or direction of introduction events to be determined conclusively. The high sequencing depth and extensive recovery of the viral segments provided sufficient resolution for HA clade assignment, whole-genome genotyping, and phylogeographic inference.All genomes reported in this study were assigned to H5 clade 2.3.4.4b. This clade has undergone rapid intercontinental expansion. Following its transatlantic introduction from Europe, the virus was detected in North America in late 2021, became established in wild birds, reassorted with locally circulating avian influenza viruses, and subsequently spread into Central and South America during 2022 (Caliendo et al., 2022; Alkie et al., 2023; Youk et al., 2023b; Leguia et al., 2023). The detection of clade 2.3.4.4b viruses in Ecuador adds to the evidence of H5N1 dissemination along the eastern Pacific coast of South America and highlights the importance of continued genomic surveillance in coastal and migratory birds.Our four genomes were assigned to genotype B3.2, with the segment constellation am2.1|am1.2|ea1|ea1|am1.4.1|ea1|ea1|am1.1. This genotype arose through reassortment between the Eurasian-origin H5N1 virus introduced into North America and low-pathogenicity avian influenza viruses circulating among North American wild birds, resulting in a mosaic genome containing Eurasian and North American lineage segments (Youk et al., 2023a; Uhart et al., 2024). B3.2 was subsequently detected during the early southward expansion of H5N1 along the Pacific coast of South America. In Peru, viruses with this reassortant genome constellation were identified in pelicans, cormorants, sanderlings, South American sea lions, and a dolphin during mortality events beginning in November 2022 (Leguia et al., 2023). Peruvian viruses also formed a monophyletic group with sequences from Chile, consistent with regional dissemination along the eastern Pacific coast (Castro-Sanguinetti et al., 2024).The exploratory phylogenetic reconstruction shown in Figure 3 provided the initial broader genetic context for the Ecuadorian detections. Among the 2,314 H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b genotype B3.2 sequences analyzed, seven genetically defined clusters were identified. Despite sharing the same genotype assignment, the Ecuadorian sequences were distributed across two distinct genetic contexts. The wild seabird viruses analyzed in this study clustered within the CHL–ECU–PER group and were most closely related to viruses from Peru. In contrast, sequences previously obtained from domestic birds in Ecuador were located in the separate COL–CAN–ECU–O.C.A.–USA group and showed a closer genetic association with viruses from the United States. This pattern suggests that the B3.2 viruses detected in Ecuador belong to distinct phylogenetic backgrounds. The separation between the wild seabird and domestic-bird sequences is compatible with independent introduction events through different geographic or ecological pathways, although alternative explanations, including unsampled transmission links and regional sampling imbalance, cannot be excluded (Lemey et al., 2020).The subsequent focused phylogenetic reconstruction further resolved the relationships among the four Ecuadorian wild seabird viruses. The viruses did not form a single monophyletic group: Cluster 1, as designated in Figure 3B, comprised the two F. magnificens viruses and had a most recent common ancestor estimated in early January 2023, whereas Cluster 2 comprised the two S. nebouxii viruses and had a most recent common ancestor estimated in early April 2023. These estimates represent the inferred timing of the common ancestry of each sampled cluster and should not be interpreted as exact dates of viral introduction into Ecuador. Peru was reconstructed as the most probable ancestral geographic state for both clusters, with posterior probabilities exceeding 0.98. However, this inference may have been influenced by uneven regional sampling and does not exclude unsampled intermediate transmission events or additional introduction pathways. Given that only four Ecuadorian genomes were analyzed, the two distinct Ecuadorian lineages represent the phylogenetic pattern supported by the available genomic data and should not be interpreted as a definitive estimate of the total number of introduction events.The ecology of the affected hosts provides a plausible framework for repeated exposure to viruses circulating along the eastern Pacific coast. Both F. magnificens and S. nebouxii are colonial seabirds that use coastal or island resting and breeding sites and may overlap with multispecies assemblages in productive marine feeding areas. Frigatebirds can forage across extensive marine areas (Giambalvo et al., 2022), whereas breeding blue-footed boobies in northern Peru have been documented travelling tens of kilometers from their colonies during individual foraging trips (Zavalaga et al., 2008). Colonial aggregation, overlap at feeding and resting sites, and contact with infected birds or contaminated environments may facilitate influenza transmission among susceptible seabirds (Lang et al., 2016; Klaassen and Wille, 2023; Couty et al., 2026). However, the present data do not identify which species introduced, amplified, or maintained the virus. Instead, they indicate that both hosts were affected within broader coastal circulation and that their viruses were associated with distinct phylogenetic histories, with no evidence of host-associated reassortment in this limited dataset.FluServer identified 29 amino acid substitutions previously associated with virulence, receptor specificity, antigenic change, polymerase activity, or antiviral resistance. However, these findings represent literature-based computational annotations rather than experimentally validated phenotypes in the Ecuadorian B3.2 viruses, because effects reported in other subtypes, viral backbones, hosts, or experimental systems may not be directly transferable (Davis et al., 2014; Suttie et al., 2019). In the PB2 segment, neither E627K nor D701N was detected, distinguishing the Ecuadorian viruses from some H5N1 viruses identified in South American marine mammals that carried markers previously associated with mammalian adaptation (Uhart et al., 2024; Tomás et al., 2024; Pardo-Roa et al., 2025). Similarly, the biological relevance of HA-S171D should be interpreted cautiously, because receptor recognition and transmissibility depend on combinations of receptor-binding-site residues, receptor avidity, HA stability, and HA–NA functional balance rather than on a single substitution (Yamada et al., 2006; Imai et al., 2012; Herfst et al., 2012). Moreover, the absence of HA-Q226L and HA-G228S, using H3-equivalent numbering, provides no molecular evidence of the canonical shift toward preferential recognition of human-type α2,6-linked sialic acids. In the M segment, M2-S31N was detected; unlike most of the other annotations, this substitution is strongly supported as a determinant of resistance to amantadine and rimantadine (Hurt et al., 2007; Pielak et al., 2009; Govorkova et al., 2013). full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionHighly pathogenic avian influenza HPAI-A(H5N1) viruses are a major global concern because of their impacts on animal health, biodiversity, and poultry production, as well as their potential risk to human health. These viruses have been recognized for their pandemic potential since the early 2000s (Peiris et al., 2007). The ancestral A/goose/Guangdong/1/1996 virus was first identified in domestic geese in Guangdong Province, China, in 1996 and later diversified into several genetic clades and genotypes (Xu et al., 1999). Among them, clade 2.3.4.4b has reached an unprecedented geographic and host range. Since 2020, viruses from this clade have spread across Europe, Africa, Asia, and the Americas, reaching North America through transatlantic movements of wild birds in late 2021 (Wille and Barr, 2022; Caliendo et al., 2022; Xie et al., 2023; Bellido-Martín et al., 2026). Over the course of the current panzootic, A(H5N1) viruses have caused extensive outbreaks in poultry, unprecedented mortality among wild birds, and an increasing number of infections in mammalian species (Couty et al., 2026; Bellido-Martín et al., 2026). Their circulation in wild-bird populations and movement along interconnected migratory flyways have contributed to the long-distance spread of the virus and its introduction into previously unaffected regions (Couty et al., 2026; Bellido-Martín et al., 2026). HPAI-A(H5N1) activity remains widespread: between 2025 and 2026, more than 2,000 outbreaks were reported by 64 countries and territories, resulting in the death or culling of more than 140 million poultry (World Organisation for Animal Health, 2026).Human infections with HPAI-A(H5N) remain uncommon despite the virus’s widespread circulation in animals, but they continue to highlight its enzootic and zoonotic potential. As of July 7, 2026, the World Health Organization had recorded 1,000 laboratory-confirmed human infections with A(H5N1), including 479 deaths, since 2003 (World Health Organization, 2026a). Most infections have occurred after direct or indirect exposure to infected animals or contaminated environments; sustained human-to-human transmission has not been documented (World Health Organization, 2026a,b).The expansion of H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b into South America marked a new stage of the panzootic. The virus was first detected in the region in Colombia in October 2022, then spread rapidly through several countries (Leguia et al., 2023; Artuso et al., 2025). Its arrival was followed by outbreaks in poultry and extensive mortality among wild birds, particularly along the Pacific coast. In Peru and Chile, Peruvian pelicans, boobies, cormorants, and other seabirds were among the most visibly affected species (Leguia et al., 2023; Cruz et al., 2023; Ulloa et al., 2023). The impact was not limited to birds. Infections and mass mortality were also reported in South American sea lions (Otaria flavescens) and other marine mammals, revealing the broad host range of the virus and its capacity to affect coastal ecosystems where birds and mammals gather in large numbers (Leguia et al., 2023; Cruz et al., 2023; Ulloa et al., 2023; Rimondi et al., 2024).Ecuador confirmed HPAI-A(H5N1) outbreaks in poultry and wild birds during this regional expansion. In January 2023, the country also reported the first human infection with an avian influenza A(H5) virus in Latin America and the Caribbean (World Health Organization, 2023). Ecuador lies along the Pacific Americas Flyway and includes continental coastal habitats and oceanic ecosystems that support large populations of migratory and resident seabirds. These populations may contribute to the introduction and movement of avian influenza viruses between breeding, feeding, and resting areas. However, genomic information of viruses sampled from wild birds in Ecuador remains limited, making it difficult to reconstruct viral introduction routes and determine how viruses detected in the country are related to those circulating elsewhere in the Americas.In this study, through a One Health framework between the National Institute for Public Health Research—Ecuador (INSPI) and the Ministry of Environment and Energy—Ecuador (MAE), we report the detection and genomic characterization of HPAI-A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b viruses from four individuals of two species of Ecuador’s seabirds: two frigatebirds (Fregata magnificens) and two blue-footed boobies (Sula nebouxii). Using whole-genome sequencing, phylogenetic and phylogeographic analyses, we investigated the origins and spatiotemporal pathways through which these viruses entered the country and assessed their relationships with viruses circulating in other parts of the Americas. We also examined amino acid substitutions previously associated with relevant biological characteristics of HPAI-A(H5N1) viruses. 2.1Sample collectionTracheal swab samples were collected from four individuals of two seabird species in Ecuador: two frigatebirds (F. magnificens), one sick and one found dead, sampled in San Vicente, Manabí Province in January 2023; and two sick blue-footed boobies (S. nebouxii) sampled in General Villamil Playas, Guayas Province in May 2023 (Figures 1A–C). Sampling was conducted by the Ministry of Environment and Energy (Ministerio de Ambiente y Energía) (Supplementary material 1).Figure 1(A) Frigatebird (Fregata magnificens) sample collection: tracheal swab. (B) Blue-footed booby (Sula nebouxii) sample collection: tracheal swab. (C) Map of Ecuador showing collection points: San Vicente-Manabí and Villamil Playas-Guayas.Panel A shows individuals in blue protective suits handling a large black bird with a red throat pouch, while the adjacent image shows close-up handling of the bird’s foot, Frigatebird. Panel B displays a seabird with blue feet standing on rocks, followed by gloved hands collecting a sample from the bird’s beak, Blue-footed booby. Panel C is a color-coded map of Ecuador, including the Galapagos Islands, with two marked locations on the Pacific Coast indicating sampling sites in Manabí and Santa Elena, and a legend categorizing regions by Pacific Coast, Andes, Amazon basin, and Galapagos. 2.2Diagnostic confirmation, genotyping, and whole-genome sequencingTracheal swab samples were initially tested for influenza A(H5N1) virus by RT-qPCR at LABIGEN, a private laboratory located in Quito. Diagnostic confirmation and genotyping were subsequently performed at the INSPI, Quito headquarters. Samples were confirmed as positive for influenza A(H5) virus by RT-qPCR at the Zonal Laboratory for Influenza and Other Respiratory Viruses. Whole-genome sequencing and bioinformatic analyses were conducted at the National Reference Center for Genomics, Sequencing and Bioinformatics (Centro de Referencia Nacional de Genómica, Secuenciación y Bioinformática, CRN-GENSBIO). Sequencing was performed on an Illumina MiSeq instrument using the Illumina Respiratory Virus Oligo Panel (RVOP) and a MiSeq v2 150-cycle reagent kit (Illumina, Inc., n.d.). The quality of the FASTQ files was evaluated using FastQC (Andrews, 2010), and adapter sequences and low-quality bases were removed using Trimmomatic (Bolger et al., 2014). Filtered reads were mapped using Bowtie2 v2.5.1 (Langmead and Salzberg, 2012) against the eight genomic segments of the influenza A/goose/Guangdong/1/1996 (H5N1) reference virus: PB2 (NC_007357.1), PB1 (NC_007358.1), PA (NC_007359.1), HA (NC_007362.1), NP (NC_007360.1), NA (NC_007361.1), M (NC_007363.1), and NS (NC_007364.1). Consensus sequences were generated from the mapped reads. Four whole-genome sequences, one from each sampled bird, were obtained and deposited in GISAID under accession numbers EPI_ISL_17973443, EPI_ISL_17973458, EPI_ISL_18137626, and EPI_ISL_18137671. 2.3Neuraminidase subtype, clade, and genotype assignmentThe neuraminidase subtype was determined by sequence similarity searches using the Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (BLAST) and the Bacterial and Viral Bioinfor…

full_text: Disclaimer: Early release articles are not considered as final versions. Any changes will be reflected in the online version in the month the article is officially released. Volume 32, Number 11—November 2026 Research Letter Evidence of Exposure to Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza H5 Viruses in East Greenland Polar Bears Suggested citation for this article Abstract We detected influenza A virus antibodies in plasma collected from East Greenland polar bears during subsistence hunts in 2024 (3/14 [21%]) and 2025 (6/14 [43%]). Four bears from 2025 had antibodies for the globally emerging highly pathogenic avian influenza virus H5 clade 2.3.4.4b, consistent with survival after exposure. Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) is an emerging ecologic and public health threat in the Arctic (1). Seasonal bird migrations to Arctic nesting grounds create a hot spot for HPAI outbreaks, amplifying interspecies interactions and the risk for viral reassortment and dissemination across migratory flyways (1). Recent detection of HPAI in wild Arctic mammals, along with their nutritional and cultural relevance for Indigenous peoples, emphasizes a strong need for surveillance in Arctic ecosystems (2–4). Polar bears (Ursus maritimus) are Arctic apex predators that face increased challenges associated with their ecologic position at the interface between marine and terrestrial ecosystems. Climate warming and the subsequent loss of sea ice leads to increased time spent on land and exposure to terrestrial pathogens through the exploitation of new food sources (5). Cases of deceased polar bears infected with HPAI have been reported in Alaska, USA (H5N1 in 2023), and Svalbard, Norway (H5N5 in 2026), emphasizing that these emerging viruses may pose a risk to Arctic species (2,6). As part of an ongoing collaboration with Indigenous hunters, heart blood was collected during subsistence harvests from polar bears that appeared healthy near Scoresby Sound (Ittoqqortoormiit) in East Greenland (Appendix Figure) during the hunting season (January–May). We screened 109 plasma samples (collected during 2016–2025) for antibodies against all influenza A viruses by using a competitive ELISA (cELISA) that targets the influenza A virus (IAV) nucleoprotein (ID Screen Influenza A Antibody Competition Multi-Species; Innovative Diagnostics, https://www.innovative-diagnostics.com), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. We detected no IAV antibodies before 2024. Three bears (all male) harvested during 2024 had signal-to-noise values within the positive range (<45%) of the cELISA (21% [95% CI 8%–48%]; n = 3/14); the number increased to 6 bears (5 male, 1 female) in 2025 (43% [95% CI 21%–67%]; n = 6/14) (Appendix Table). We conducted further screening on positive samples (n = 9) and a subset of negative samples (n = 3) by using a hemagglutination inhibition assay that used horse red blood cells (Rockland Immunochemicals, https://www.rockland.com), as described by Kayali et al. (7), with minor modifications. In brief, we heat-inactivated plasma at 56 °C for 30 minutes, then hem-adsorbed it and treated it with receptor-destroying enzyme. We used avian influenza viruses representative of H5 and H7 subtypes in the assay (Table). Plasma from 4 animals harvested in 2025 that were positive for IAV antibodies on the cELISA were positive (>1:40) for antibodies to H5N1 viruses falling within clade 2.3.4.4b on the hemagglutination inhibition assay, suggesting that the animals had been exposed to an HPAI virus in this clade (Table). We first detected IAV antibodies in East Greenland polar bears in 2024 and antibodies to the highly pathogenic H5 clade 2.3.4.4b in 2025. H5N5 and H5N1 strains were previously confirmed in sea birds (including Uria aalge [H5N1 in 2022], Larus hyperboreus [H5N5 in 2023], Fulmarus glacialis [H5N5 in 2023 and 2024], and Larus marinus [H5N5 in 2024]) from the west coast of Greenland (8,9), consistent with our findings of evidence of IAV exposure in East Greenland polar bears in 2024. Positive bears probably were exposed during the summer–fall bird migration the year before the bears were harvested, given that migratory birds are absent during the polar bear hunting season. Hunters reported no clinical signs, suggesting that bears can recover from HPAI infection. That finding is consistent with the high prevalence reported in our study and survival of the bears for months after the departure of migratory birds. Although cross-reactivity with low pathogenic H5 subtypes is possible, plasma from all 4 seropositive bears inhibited hemagglutination of viruses within clade 2.3.4.4b (not observed when tested against clade 1) (Table). That finding strongly supports infection with a virus from clade 2.3.4.4b, which is exclusively an HPAI lineage. HPAI spillover to mammalian hosts typically occurs through ingestion of infected birds or through contaminated environments (1,3,10). Transmission to wild mammals may involve multiple mechanisms, including direct contact through mucosal or nasal secretions, scavenging dead birds or bird eggs or infected mammals, and mother-to-offspring transmission through lactation (Figure) (10). Further studies are needed to identify which mechanisms are relevant for polar bears, although the most likely route is by eating dead or infected birds and mammals. Our study also highlights the strength of collaboration between scientists and local subsistence hunters, emphasizing the need for future research that incorporates diverse perspectives and cultural practices to effectively monitor the health of wildlife in these remote regions. Volume 32, Number 11—November 2026 Research Letter Evidence of Exposure to Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza H5 Viruses in East Greenland Polar Bears Suggested citation for this article Abstract We detected influenza A virus antibodies in plasma collected from East Greenland polar bears during subsistence hunts in 2024 (3/14 [21%]) and 2025 (6/14 [43%]). Four bears from 2025 had antibodies for the globally emerging highly pathogenic avian influenza virus H5 clade 2.3.4.4b, consistent with survival after exposure. Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) is an emerging ecologic and public health threat in the Arctic (1). Seasonal bird migrations to Arctic nesting grounds create a hot spot for HPAI outbreaks, amplifying interspecies interactions and the risk for viral reassortment and dissemination across migratory flyways (1). Recent detection of HPAI in wild Arctic mammals, along with their nutritional and cultural relevance for Indigenous peoples, emphasizes a strong need for surveillance in Arctic ecosystems (2–4). Polar bears (Ursus maritimus) are Arctic apex predators that face increased challenges associated with their ecologic position at the interface between marine and terrestrial ecosystems. Climate warming and the subsequent loss of sea ice leads to increased time spent on land and exposure to terrestrial pathogens through the exploitation of new food sources (5). Cases of deceased polar bears infected with HPAI have been reported in Alaska, USA (H5N1 in 2023), and Svalbard, Norway (H5N5 in 2026), emphasizing that these emerging viruses may pose a risk to Arctic species (2,6). As part of an ongoing collaboration with Indigenous hunters, heart blood was collected during subsistence harvests from polar bears that appeared healthy near Scoresby Sound (Ittoqqortoormiit) in East Greenland (Appendix Figure) during the hunting season (January–May). We screened 109 plasma samples (collected during 2016–2025) for antibodies against all influenza A viruses by using a competitive ELISA (cELISA) that targets the influenza A virus (IAV) nucleoprotein (ID Screen Influenza A Antibody Competition Multi-Species; Innovative Diagnostics, https://www.innovative-diagnostics.com), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. We detected no IAV antibodies before 2024. Three bears (all male) harvested during 2024 had signal-to-noise values within the positive range (<45%) of the cELISA (21% [95% CI 8%–48%]; n = 3/14); the number increased to 6 bears (5 male, 1 female) in 2025 (43% [95% CI 21%–67%]; n = 6/14) (Appendix Table). We conducted further screening on positive samples (n = 9) and a subset of negative samples (n = 3) by using a hemagglutination inhibition assay that used horse red blood cells (Rockland Immunochemicals, https://www.rockland.com), as described by Kayali et al. (7), with minor modifications. In brief, we heat-inactivated plasma at 56 °C for 30 minutes, then hem-adsorbed it and treated it with receptor-destroying enzyme. We used avian influenza viruses representative of H5 and H7 subtypes in the assay (Table). Plasma from 4 animals harvested in 2025 that were positive for IAV antibodies on the cELISA were positive (>1:40) for antibodies to H5N1 viruses falling within clade 2.3.4.4b on the hemagglutination inhibition assay, suggesting that the animals had been exposed to an HPAI virus in this clade (Table). We first detected IAV antibodies in East Greenland polar bears in 2024 and antibodies to the highly pathogenic H5 clade 2.3.4.4b in 2025. H5N5 and H5N1 strains were previously confirmed in sea birds (including Uria aalge [H5N1 in 2022], Larus hyperboreus [H5N5 in 2023], Fulmarus glacialis [H5N5 in 2023 and 2024], and Larus marinus [H5N5 in 2024]) from the west coast of Greenland (8,9), consistent with our findings of evidence of IAV exposure in East Greenland polar bears in 2024. Positive bears probably were exposed during the summer–fall bird migration the year before the bears were harvested, given that migratory birds are absent during the polar bear hunting season. Hunters reported no clinical signs, suggesting that bears can recover from HPAI infection. That finding is consistent with the high prevalence reported in our study and survival of the bears for months after the departure of migratory birds. Although cross-reactivity with low pathogenic H5 subtypes is possible, plasma from all 4 seropositive bears inhibited hemagglutination of viruses within clade 2.3.4.4b (not observed when tested against clade 1) (Table). That finding strongly supports infection with a virus from clade 2.3.4.4b, which is exclusively an HPAI lineage. HPAI spillover to mammalian hosts typically occurs through ingestion of infected birds or through contaminated environments (1,3,10). Greenland links the East Atlantic and the North American Atlantic flyways (Appendix Figure), and increased surveillance in this region may provide effective early warning signs of HPAI dissemination. Our findings indicate that East Greenland polar bears have been exposed to HPAI in recent years, consistent with the timeline of prior reports of HPAI in birds along the linked migratory superhighways (3,8,9). Our study also highlights the strength of collaboration between scientists and local subsistence hunters, emphasizing the need for future research that incorporates diverse perspectives and cultural practices to effectively monitor the health of wildlife in these remote regions. analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to detect antibodies to highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) in East Greenland polar bears, addressing the emerging threat of HPAI in Arctic ecosystems. The research fills a knowledge gap by identifying HPAI exposure in polar bears, which are apex predators in the Arctic and may serve as sentinels for viral spread.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved collecting heart blood samples from 109 polar bears during the hunting season (January–May) from 2016 to 2025. Samples were collected from East Greenland and analyzed for antibodies against influenza A viruses using a competitive ELISA and hemagglutination inhibition assay.
analysis.methods: Samples were screened for antibodies against all influenza A viruses using a competitive ELISA, and further testing was conducted using a hemagglutination inhibition assay with avian influenza viruses representative of H5 and H7 subtypes. The study complied with international permits for sample collection and transport.
analysis.main_results: Three bears from 2024 and six bears from 2025 had antibodies to HPAI, with signal-to-noise values within the positive range. Four of the six 2025 bears had antibodies to the highly pathogenic H5 clade 2.3.4.4b, indicating recent exposure.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study provides evidence of HPAI exposure in East Greenland polar bears, highlighting the need for increased surveillance in Arctic ecosystems. The findings suggest that polar bears may serve as sentinels for HPAI spread and emphasize the importance of collaboration between scientists and local subsistence hunters.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings caution that HPAI may pose a risk to Arctic species, including polar bears, and underscore the need for enhanced surveillance and monitoring of viral spread in these regions. analysis_zh.methods: 样本通过竞争ELISA检测针对所有流感A病毒的抗体,随后使用代表H5和H7亚型的禽流感病毒进行进一步的血凝抑制试验。本研究遵守了国际样本采集和运输许可。
analysis_zh.main_results: 2024年的三只北极熊和2025年的六只北极熊对高致病性禽流感(HPAI)有抗体,信号与噪音比值处于阳性范围内。2025年的六只北极熊中有四只对高致病性H5亚型2.3.4.4b病毒有抗体,表明近期暴露。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 本研究提供了东格陵兰北极熊暴露于高致病性禽流感(HPAI)的证据,强调了在北极生态系统中增加监测监测的必要性。研究结果表明,北极熊可能作为HPAI传播的哨兵,并突显了科学家与当地生存狩猎者合作的重要性。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果警示高致病性禽流感(HPAI)可能对北极物种(包括北极熊)构成风险,并强调了在这些地区加强监测监测和病毒传播监控的必要性。此外,本研究还突显了科学家与当地狩猎者合作在监测野生动物健康方面的价值。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究的局限性在于样本量较小,以及可能与低致病性H5亚型发生交叉反应。然而,研究结果得到了抗体高患病率水平和北极熊暴露后存活的有力支持,表明其证据基础较强。}}.

title: A comprehensive high-throughput detection strategy: an indirect ELISA for serodetection of the novel aMPV/C in ducks

source_records.title: A comprehensive high-throughput detection strategy: an indirect ELISA for serodetection of the novel aMPV/C in ducks

priority_tier_reason: 补充性记录、预印本或证据完整度有限
full_text: AbstractIntroductionAvian metapneumovirus subtype C (aMPV/C), a re-emerging and widespread epidemic in China, causes hydrosalpinx fluid syndrome (HFS) in laying ducks, resulting in significant economic losses to the poultry industry. In the absence of any licensed vaccines or antiviral drugs for aMPV/C, accurate diagnosis and timely eradication of the infected ducks remain the primary control measures, underscoring the urgent need for reliable and effective detection methods.MethodsIn this study, the purified whole novel aMPV/C was used to develop an indirect enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (iELISA) for the detection of aMPV/C antibodies in ducks.ResultsThe cut-off value of the iELISA was determined to be 0.258. No cross-reactivity was observed with duck sera positive for antibodies against H5 AIV, NDV, DTMUV, BTV, DHAV-3, DPV, EDSV, MDPV, or GPV, demonstrating good specificity. Both intra-assay and inter-assay coefficients of variation were less than 10%, and the detection sensitivity of the iELISA reached a serum dilution of 1:102400. A total of 216 clinical serum samples from three duck breeds were tested via the established iELISA, of which 129 (59.7%) were positive. The concordance rate between the iELISA and an indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA) was 100% (53/53).ConclusionOverall, this cost-effective iELISA provides a reliable tool for the detection of aMPV/C antibodies in clinical diagnostics and epidemiological surveillance.Keywords: avian metapneumovirus subtype C, novel, ducks, indirect ELISA, serological detection Materials and methodsVirus purificationThe aMPV/C isolate (aMPV-FJ21, 106.56 TCID50/mL) maintained in our laboratory was used in this study (Fu et al., 2025). Vero cells were inoculated with the virus, maintained in serum-free medium, and harvested at 96 h post-infection (hpi), followed by storage at −70 °C. The harvested cells were subjected to three cycles of freezing and thawing. The virus was then inactivated with 0.1% formaldehyde at 37 °C overnight. For antigen purification, 300 mL of inactivated suspension was clarified by centrifugation at 10000 × g for 15 min at 4 °C to remove cellular debris. Subsequently, the virus suspension was pelleted by ultracentrifugation at 45000 × g for 5 h. The resulting pellet was resuspended in 1 mL of 0.01 M phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, pH7.4) and used as the coating antigen for ELISA development. Meanwhile, the purified virus was examined using a transmission electron microscope (TEM, H-7500, Hitachi, Japan). And its protein concentration was determined using the enhanced BCA protein assay kit (Beyotime Biotechnology China, Fuzhou, China).Generation of polyclonal antibody against aMPV/CPurified aMPV-FJ21 strain, emulsified with an equal volume of Freund’s complete adjuvant (Sigma-Aldrich, Kenilworth, United States), was used as the immunogen for polyclonal antibody production. Sheldrake ducks were immunized with 1 mL immunogen via multiple subcutaneous injections in the dorsal region, with a negative control group included in parallel. Immunizations were administered at 2-week intervals for a total of four doses. The primary immunization used Freund’s complete adjuvant, whereas the three subsequent booster doses employed Freund’s incomplete adjuvant. Serum samples were collected 2 weeks after the final immunization for subsequent analysis.Establishment of the whole aMPV/C virus-based iELISACheckerboard titrationOptimal iELISA conditions were determined by checkerboard titration. Briefly, 96-well plates (Corning, New York, United States) were coated with 100 μL/well of purified aMPV-FJ21 at concentrations of 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 and 0.5 μg/mL in carbonate buffer (CBS, 0.05 M, pH 9.6) at 37 °C for 1 h. After three washes with PBS containing 0.05% (v/v) Tween 20 (PBST), plates were blocked with 10% skimmed milk in PBS at 37 °C for 2 h, followed by three additional washes. aMPV/C-positive and aMPV/C-negative duck sera, serially diluted from 1:100 to 1:3200 in PBS, were added (100 μL/well) and incubated at 37 °C for 1 h. Plates were washed, and 100 μL of horseradish peroxidase-conjugated goat anti-duck IgG antibody (1:10000, KPL, Maryland, United States) was added, followed by incubation at 37 °C for 1 h. After washing, 100 μL of TMB substrate (Solarbio, Beijing, China) was added and incubated at 37 °C for 10 min. The reaction was stopped with 50 μL/well of stop solution, and the optical density was measured at 450 nm (OD450nm) using an automatic ELISA reader (SpectraMax M3, Molecular Devices, USA). The optimal conditions were selected based on the highest positive-to-negative (P/N) ratio.Optimization of experimental parametersTo determine optimal coating conditions, different coating times (overnight at 4 °C; 1, 2 and 3 h at 37 °C) and coating solutions (normal saline, PBS, CBS, and ddH2O) were evaluated. The iELISA was then performed to optimize blocking times (60, 90, 120, and 150 min at 37 °C) and blocking solutions (1, 2% BSA, 5, 10% skimmed milk, and 10% FBS). Next, antibody–antigen reaction times, various incubation periods (30, 60, 90, and 120 min at 37 °C) and dilutions of the enzyme-labeled secondary antibody (1:2000, 1:4000, 1:5000, 1:8000, and 1:10000) were tested. Finally, TMB reaction times (5, 10, 15, 20, and 25 min at 37 °C) was evaluated to identify the optimal assay conditions.Determination of the cut-off valueTo determine the cut-off value for the iELISA, 57 serum samples from healthy ducks (negative for aMPV/C) were used. The cut-off was calculated based on the mean and standard deviation (SD) of the OD450nm values obtained from negative samples. It was defined as the mean OD450nm of the 57 negative sera plus 3SD, a threshold that theoretically provides >99% confidence that results from true negative samples fell below this value.Specificity and repeatabilityThe specificity of the iELISA was evaluated using positive sera against H5 avian influenza virus (H5 AIV, titer: 7log2), Newcastle disease virus (NDV, titer: 6log2), egg drop syndrome virus (EDSV, titer: 6log2), duck Tembusu virus (DTMUV, titer: 1:512), duck plague virus (DPV, titer: 1:640), Batai virus (BTV, titer: 1:256), Muscovy duck parvovirus (MDPV, titer: 1:512), goose parvovirus (GPV, titer: 1:640), and duck hepatitis A virus type 3 (DHAV-3, titer: 1:1024). Antibody titers against H5 AIV, NDV, and EDSV were assessed using hemagglutination inhibition (HI) assay, whereas titers against DTMUV, DPV, BTV, MDPV, GPV, and DHAV-3 were evaluated by iELISA. aMPV/C-positive and aMPV/C-negative sera were included as controls.To assess the repeatability of the iELISA, four aMPV/C-positive and four aMPV/C-negative sera were randomly selected and tested in triplicate on both the same batch and different batches of ELISA plates. Variability was expressed as the coefficient of variation (CV), calculated as the standard deviation (SD) divided by the mean optical density at OD450nm for each sample group.Sensitivity of the iELISAThe sensitivity of the iELISA was evaluated using twofold serial dilutions of three aMPV/C-positive serum with different OD450nm, ranging from 1:100 to 1:204800, in a parallel assay.IFAThe viral antigen was detected by IFA during this period as described by Fu et al. (2025). Briefly, Vero cells in 96-well plates (105 cells/well) were infected with the aMPV-FJ21 strain (105TCID50) for 72 h. Following infection, cells were fixed with pre-cooled 4% paraformaldehyde (Sigma-Aldrich, Kenilworth, USA) in PBS for 15 min at 4 °C and permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100 (Sigma-Aldrich, Kenilworth, USA) in PBS containing 2% BSA (Beyotime, Shanghai, China) for 30 min. The fixed cells were then incubated with test serum (1:100) as the primary antibody for 1.5 h at 37 °C. aMPV/C-negative serum served as a mock control. After washing with PBST, the cells were incubated with Alexa Fluor 488-labeled goat anti-duck IgG (1:200, KPL, Maryland, United States) for 1 h at 37 °C.
