full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractIntroductionAvian metapneumovirus subtype C (aMPV/C), a re-emerging and widespread epidemic in China, causes hydrosalpinx fluid syndrome (HFS) in laying ducks, resulting in significant economic losses to the poultry industry. In the absence of any licensed vaccines or antiviral drugs for aMPV/C, accurate diagnosis and timely eradication of the infected ducks remain the primary control measures, underscoring the urgent need for reliable and effective detection methods.MethodsIn this study, the purified whole novel aMPV/C was used to develop an indirect enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (iELISA) for the detection of aMPV/C antibodies in ducks.ResultsThe cut-off value of the iELISA was determined to be 0.258. No cross-reactivity was observed with duck sera positive for antibodies against H5 AIV, NDV, DTMUV, BTV, DHAV-3, DPV, EDSV, MDPV, or GPV, demonstrating good specificity. Both intra-assay and inter-assay coefficients of variation were less than 10%, and the detection sensitivity of the iELISA reached a serum dilution of 1:102400. A total of 216 clinical serum samples from three duck breeds were tested via the established iELISA, of which 129 (59.7%) were positive. The concordance rate between the iELISA and an indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA) was 100% (53/53).ConclusionOverall, this cost-effective iELISA provides a reliable tool for the detection of aMPV/C antibodies in clinical diagnostics and epidemiological surveillance.Keywords: avian metapneumovirus subtype C, novel, ducks, indirect ELISA, serological detection
full_text_sections.methods: Materials and methodsVirus purificationThe aMPV/C isolate (aMPV-FJ21, 106.56 TCID50/mL) maintained in our laboratory was used in this study (Fu et al., 2025). Vero cells were inoculated with the virus, maintained in serum-free medium, and harvested at 96 h post-infection (hpi), followed by storage at −70 °C. The harvested cells were subjected to three cycles of freezing and thawing. The virus was then inactivated with 0.1% formaldehyde at 37 °C overnight. For antigen purification, 300 mL of inactivated suspension was clarified by centrifugation at 10000 × g for 15 min at 4 °C to remove cellular debris. Subsequently, the virus suspension was pelleted by ultracentrifugation at 45000 × g for 5 h. The resulting pellet was resuspended in 1 mL of 0.01 M phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, pH7.4) and used as the coating antigen for ELISA development. Meanwhile, the purified virus was examined using a transmission electron microscope (TEM, H-7500, Hitachi, Japan). And its protein concentration was determined using the enhanced BCA protein assay kit (Beyotime Biotechnology China, Fuzhou, China).Generation of polyclonal antibody against aMPV/CPurified aMPV-FJ21 strain, emulsified with an equal volume of Freund’s complete adjuvant (Sigma-Aldrich, Kenilworth, United States), was used as the immunogen for polyclonal antibody production. Sheldrake ducks were immunized with 1 mL immunogen via multiple subcutaneous injections in the dorsal region, with a negative control group included in parallel. Immunizations were administered at 2-week intervals for a total of four doses. The primary immunization used Freund’s complete adjuvant, whereas the three subsequent booster doses employed Freund’s incomplete adjuvant. Serum samples were collected 2 weeks after the final immunization for subsequent analysis.Establishment of the whole aMPV/C virus-based iELISACheckerboard titrationOptimal iELISA conditions were determined by checkerboard titration. Briefly, 96-well plates (Corning, New York, United States) were coated with 100 μL/well of purified aMPV-FJ21 at concentrations of 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 and 0.5 μg/mL in carbonate buffer (CBS, 0.05 M, pH 9.6) at 37 °C for 1 h. After three washes with PBS containing 0.05% (v/v) Tween 20 (PBST), plates were blocked with 10% skimmed milk in PBS at 37 °C for 2 h, followed by three additional washes. aMPV/C-positive and aMPV/C-negative duck sera, serially diluted from 1:100 to 1:3200 in PBS, were added (100 μL/well) and incubated at 37 °C for 1 h. Plates were washed, and 100 μL of horseradish peroxidase-conjugated goat anti-duck IgG antibody (1:10000, KPL, Maryland, United States) was added, followed by incubation at 37 °C for 1 h. After washing, 100 μL of TMB substrate (Solarbio, Beijing, China) was added and incubated at 37 °C for 10 min. The reaction was stopped with 50 μL/well of stop solution, and the optical density was measured at 450 nm (OD450nm) using an automatic ELISA reader (SpectraMax M3, Molecular Devices, USA). The optimal conditions were selected based on the highest positive-to-negative (P/N) ratio.Optimization of experimental parametersTo determine optimal coating conditions, different coating times (overnight at 4 °C; 1, 2 and 3 h at 37 °C) and coating solutions (normal saline, PBS, CBS, and ddH2O) were evaluated. The iELISA was then performed to optimize blocking times (60, 90, 120, and 150 min at 37 °C) and blocking solutions (1, 2% BSA, 5, 10% skimmed milk, and 10% FBS). Next, antibody–antigen reaction times, various incubation periods (30, 60, 90, and 120 min at 37 °C) and dilutions of the enzyme-labeled secondary antibody (1:2000, 1:4000, 1:5000, 1:8000, and 1:10000) were tested. Finally, TMB reaction times (5, 10, 15, 20, and 25 min at 37 °C) was evaluated to identify the optimal assay conditions.Determination of the cut-off valueTo determine the cut-off value for the iELISA, 57 serum samples from healthy ducks (negative for aMPV/C) were used. The cut-off was calculated based on the mean and standard deviation (SD) of the OD450nm values obtained from negative samples. It was defined as the mean OD450nm of the 57 negative sera plus 3SD, a threshold that theoretically provides >99% confidence that results from true negative samples fell below this value.Specificity and repeatabilityThe specificity of the iELISA was evaluated using positive sera against H5 avian influenza virus (H5 AIV, titer: 7log2), Newcastle disease virus (NDV, titer: 6log2), egg drop syndrome virus (EDSV, titer: 6log2), duck Tembusu virus (DTMUV, titer: 1:512), duck plague virus (DPV, titer: 1:640), Batai virus (BTV, titer: 1:256), Muscovy duck parvovirus (MDPV, titer: 1:512), goose parvovirus (GPV, titer: 1:640), and duck hepatitis A virus type 3 (DHAV-3, titer: 1:1024). Antibody titers against H5 AIV, NDV, and EDSV were assessed using hemagglutination inhibition (HI) assay, whereas titers against DTMUV, DPV, BTV, MDPV, GPV, and DHAV-3 were evaluated by iELISA. aMPV/C-positive and aMPV/C-negative sera were included as controls.To assess the repeatability of the iELISA, four aMPV/C-positive and four aMPV/C-negative sera were randomly selected and tested in triplicate on both the same batch and different batches of ELISA plates. Variability was expressed as the coefficient of variation (CV), calculated as the standard deviation (SD) divided by the mean optical density at OD450nm for each sample group.Sensitivity of the iELISAThe sensitivity of the iELISA was evaluated using twofold serial dilutions of three aMPV/C-positive serum with different OD450nm, ranging from 1:100 to 1:204800, in a parallel assay.IFAThe viral antigen was detected by IFA during this period as described by Fu et al. (2025). Briefly, Vero cells in 96-well plates (105 cells/well) were infected with the aMPV-FJ21 strain (105TCID50) for 72 h. Following infection, cells were fixed with pre-cooled 4% paraformaldehyde (Sigma-Aldrich, Kenilworth, USA) in PBS for 15 min at 4 °C and permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100 (Sigma-Aldrich, Kenilworth, USA) in PBS containing 2% BSA (Beyotime, Shanghai, China) for 30 min. The fixed cells were then incubated with test serum (1:100) as the primary antibody for 1.5 h at 37 °C. aMPV/C-negative serum served as a mock control. After washing with PBST, the cells were incubated with Alexa Fluor 488-labeled goat anti-duck IgG (1:200, KPL, Maryland, United States) for 1 h at 37 °C. Finally, all samples were observed under a Nikon A1R confocal fluorescence microscope (Nikon Instruments, Inc., Melville, United States).Detection of antibodies in clinical serum samplesA total of 216 clinical serum samples from ducks exhibiting a drop in egg production or respiratory symptoms, comprising 136 from Sheldrake ducks, 42 from Muscovy ducks, and 38 from Cherry Valley ducks, were tested using the established iELISA. Subsequently, 53 of these samples were randomly selected for detection by IFA, and the concordance rate between the two methods was calculated.Statistical analysisEach experiment was carried out in at least three independent replicates. Significant differences were determined using t-tests and non-parametric tests in GraphPad 8.0, with a significance level set of p < 0.05.

full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionSince Although aMPV subtype B has historically been the dominant lineage in Chinese poultry, the epidemiological landscape has shifted considerably since 2021, with aMPV/C now emerging as a significant pathogen in domestic duck populations (Fu et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2022). This epidemiological transition is particularly noteworthy given that aMPV/C was first detected in ducks in 2014 but remained largely unreported in waterfowl for nearly a decade, suggesting that the virus may have undergone adaptive changes that facilitated its spread and establishment in duck hosts (Sun et al., 2014). The recent identification of a novel aMPV/C lineage in Sheldrake ducks is especially concerning, as this variant appears to have acquired a distinct tropism for reproductive tissues, manifesting as hydrosalpinx fluid syndrome rather than the classical respiratory disease typically associated with aMPV infections (Fu et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2024). This clinical shift from respiratory to reproductive pathology may reflect ongoing viral evolution and adaptation to new host species, potentially involving changes in the viral attachment protein or other surface glycoproteins that determine cell tropism. Furthermore, the seasonal recurrence of this disease on affected farms, often correlated with annual climatic variations, complicates disease control efforts and underscores the urgent need for diagnostic tools that are both reliable and broadly applicable across different duck breeds and production systems (Fu et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2014).Historically, aMPV subtypes A, B, and C have predominantly circulated in chickens and turkeys worldwide (Cook, 2000; Salles et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2013). Consequently, numerous indirect ELISAs using various structural proteins (N, M, F, and G) as coating antigens have been developed for serological surveillance in these species (Chiang et al., 2000; Gulati et al., 2000; Gulati et al., 2001; Alvarez et al., 2004; Xu et al., 2021). However, no commercial ELISA kit is currently available for detecting aMPV antibodies in duck sera, particularly against subtype C. To address this diagnostic gap, we developed an iELISA using whole inactivated aMPV/C virions as the coating antigen. This approach offers distinct advantages over recombinant protein-based assays, which have been the standard for aMPV serology in chickens and turkeys. While recombinant proteins are widely adopted due to their ease of production and scalability, they often fail to present the full repertoire of conformational and linear epitopes present on native viral particles, and interference from components of the prokaryotic expression host (Escherichia coli), potentially compromising assay sensitivity and leading to false-negative results, especially in low-titer samples (Meireles et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2026). In contrast, whole-virion antigens preserve the native antigenic architecture, enabling more comprehensive detection across a broader range of antibody specificities and isotypes (Sumita et al., 2016). This feature is particularly valuable for detecting antibodies against emerging viral variants, as a single recombinant protein may not adequately capture the antigenic diversity of circulating strains. The aMPV-FJ21 strain used in this study achieved high titers in Vero cells, substantially exceeding previously reported levels at the same passage, thereby providing ample antigen for large-scale production while ensuring consistent quality (Sun et al., 2014; Yao et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2023). The use of a single master seed stock, combined with serum-free culture conditions and rigorous control of passage number and culture parameters, further ensured batch- to-batch consistency and minimized the risk of exogenous protein contamination that could otherwise compromise assay specificity.The analytical performance of the iELISA was robust and met the requirements for a practical diagnostic tool. No cross-reactivity was observed against sera positive for nine other major duck pathogens, including H5 AIV, NDV, EDSV, DTMUV, DPV, BTV, MDPV, GPV, and DHAV-3, demonstrating high specificity. This specificity is critical for accurate diagnosis in field settings where co-infections with multiple pathogens are common. The detection limit of 1:102400 indicates high sensitivity, making the assay suitable for detecting low-titer antibodies in field samples, particularly during the early stages of infection or in vaccinated flocks where antibody levels may be relatively low. The excellent reproducibility of the assay, with coefficients of variation below 10% in both intra- and inter-assay evaluations, confirms its operational stability and reliability for routine diagnostic use across different laboratories and operators.Application of the iELISA to 216 clinical serum samples collected from three duck breeds revealed an overall seroprevalence of 59.7%, with notable variation among breeds: Sheldrake ducks showed the highest positivity rate (69.1%), followed by Muscovy ducks (57.1%) and Cherry Valley ducks (28.9%). This breed-dependent variation may reflect differences in genetic susceptibility, management practices, or environmental exposure, and warrants further investigation into the host factors that influence aMPV/C infection dynamics. The higher seroprevalence observed in Sheldrake and Muscovy ducks compared to Cherry Valley ducks could be related to breed-specific differences in receptor expression, immune response efficiency, or husbandry practices that affect virus transmission. The complete concordance (100%) between the iELISA and IFA in a subset of 53 samples further validates the reliability of the assay and supports its utility as a practical tool for large-scale serological surveillance. This high level of agreement suggests that the iELISA can be used interchangeably with IFA, offering the advantages of higher throughput, objective readout, and reduced labor intensity, making it particularly suitable for epidemiological surveys and routine monitoring programs in commercial duck farms. These findings collectively support the suitability of the developed iELISA for large-scale serological surveillance of aMPV/C infection in duck flocks, providing a valuable tool for disease monitoring and control efforts.
full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionIn summary, we developed a sensitive, specific, and reproducible iELISA for detecting aMPV/C antibodies in duck sera, demonstrating 100% concordance with IFA. This assay provides a practical tool for large-scale serological surveillance. The widespread seropositivity across duck breeds highlights the urgent need for vaccination strategies and routine monitoring to mitigate the impact of aMPV/C on China’s duck industry.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionAvian metapneumovirus (aMPV) was first identified in South Africa in 1978 (Buys and Preez, 1980) and has since become a globally distributed pathogen, infecting both domestic poultry and wild avian species (Salles et al., 2023). The virus causes upper respiratory disease, typically characterized by sinusitis, head swelling, and decreased egg production (Clontz and Hoerr, 2026; De Graaf et al., 2009). In uncomplicated cases, mortality is generally low (2–5%); however, co-infections with secondary pathogens can elevate mortality to as high as 25%. Based on genetic and antigenic variability, aMPV is classified into four subtypes (A-D) (Juhasz and Easton, 1994; Bäyon-Auboyer et al., 2000; Rima et al., 2017). Subtypes A and B are distributed worldwide, with subtype B predominating in Europe and China (Franzo et al., 2020). Subtype C naturally infects turkeys, chickens, ducks, and wild birds, and its genome exhibits the highest homology with human metapneumovirus (Hatfield et al., 2026). Prior to 2025, aMPV/C was known to comprise two distinct lineages: the North American and the Eurasian lineages (Quan et al., 2020). Recently, our group identified a novel lineage circulating in Sheldrake ducks (Fu et al., 2025). In contrast, subtype D has only been reported in France (Umar et al., 2019). Notably, two novel and divergent aMPV strains were detected in North America in 2019, further highlighting the ongoing expansion of aMPV genetic diversity (Canuti et al., 2019; Retallack et al., 2019).In China, aMPV/C was first recorded in Muscovy ducks in 2014, with no subsequent isolations from waterfowl reported until 2021 (Sun et al., 2014). Since then, the virus has become increasingly prevalent nationwide, causing hydrosalpinx fluid syndrome (HFS) in laying ducks and respiratory disease in meat ducks (Yu et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2025). In 2025, we isolated a novel strain, designated aMPV-FJ21, from Sheldrake ducks exhibiting HFS (Fu et al., 2025). Molecular characterization revealed that this strain is genetically distinct from both the North American and Eurasian lineages, indicating ongoing genetic diversification and adaptive evolution of aMPV/C in China (Fu et al., 2025). These findings underscore the urgent need for effective control measures, particularly rapid and reliable diagnostic tools.Current diagnostic approaches for aMPV/C include pathogen isolation, molecular assays, and serological tests. Virus isolation is labor-intensive and time-consuming, and its recovery rate from clinical samples is notoriously low, reported as only 8% (2/25), rendering it impractical for routine clinical diagnosis (Kwon et al., 2010; Sun et al., 2014). Molecular methods, such as PCR, offer high specificity and sensitivity but require specialized equipment and skilled personnel (Shin et al., 2000). Moreover, their diagnostic utility is constrained by the short viremic window of aMPV/C, typically lasting only 2–10 days post-infection (Cook et al., 1993; Cook et al., 2001). Serological assays, including virus neutralization tests (VNT), IFA, and ELISA, are widely employed for antibody detection (Chiang et al., 2000). Among these, ELISA is particularly suitable for large-scale surveillance due to its high throughput, sensitivity, and specificity, and remains a cornerstone for monitoring infection pressure, assessing flock immunity, and guiding vaccination strategies (Saeed et al., 2026). However, to date, no commercial ELISA kit is available for the detection of aMPV/C antibodies in duck sera.To bridge this diagnostic gap, we developed an iELISA using a purified novel aMPV/C isolate as the coating antigen, specifically designed for the detection of aMPV/C antibodies in duck sera. This assay offers a practical and reliable tool for the diagnosis and epidemiological surveillance of aMPV/C infection in ducks, with the potential to support disease control efforts in affected regions. Virus purificationThe aMPV/C isolate (aMPV-FJ21, 106.56 TCID50/mL) maintained in our laboratory was used in this study (Fu et al., 2025). Vero cells were inoculated with the virus, maintained in serum-free medium, and harvested at 96 h post-infection (hpi), followed by storage at −70 °C. The harvested cells were subjected to three cycles of freezing and thawing. The virus was then inactivated with 0.1% formaldehyde at 37 °C overnight. For antigen purification, 300 mL of inactivated suspension was clarified by centrifugation at 10000 × g for 15 min at 4 °C to remove cellular debris. Subsequently, the virus suspension was pelleted by ultracentrifugation at 45000 × g for 5 h. The resulting pellet was resuspended in 1 mL of 0.01 M phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, pH7.4) and used as the coating antigen for ELISA development. Meanwhile, the purified virus was examined using a transmission electron microscope (TEM, H-7500, Hitachi, Japan). And its protein concentration was determined using the enhanced BCA protein assay kit (Beyotime Biotechnology China, Fuzhou, China). Generation of polyclonal antibody against aMPV/CPurified aMPV-FJ21 strain, emulsified with an equal volume of Freund’s complete adjuvant (Sigma-Aldrich, Kenilworth, United States), was used as the immunogen for polyclonal antibody production. Sheldrake ducks were immunized with 1 mL immunogen via multiple subcutaneous injections in the dorsal region, with a negative control group included in parallel. Immunizations were administered at 2-week intervals for a total of four doses. The primary immunization used Freund’s complete adjuvant, whereas the three subsequent booster doses employed Freund’s incomplete adjuvant. Serum samples were collected 2 weeks after the final immunization for subsequent analysis. Keywords: NPHI, health financing, health care delivery, health emergency, health resource, domestic funding, Eastern Mediterranean Citation: Asthana S, Khan W. Financing national public health institutes to play a better role in addressing health emergencies in the Eastern Mediterranean Region. East Mediterr Health J. 2026;32(9):573–576. https://doi.org/10.26719/2026.32.9.573. Received: 22/03/2026; Accepted: 01/06/2026 Copyright © Authors 2026; Licensee: World Health Organization. EMHJ is an open-access journal. This paper is available under the Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial ShareAlike 3.0 IGO licence (CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/3.0/igo). The WHO Eastern Mediterranean Region (EMR) includes 22 countries and territories with significant variations in health care financing. On average, EMR countries spent 4.87% of their Gross Domestic Product (GDP) on health, with Jordan allocating the highest (8.31%) and Qatar (2.29%) allocating the lowest (1). Between 2005 and 2014, Qatar ranked first in health system financing, followed by United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Kuwait, and Qatar had the highest Total Health Expenditure (THE) per capita at US$ 1733.86, while Pakistan had the lowest at US$ 31.35 (1). The region is prone to health emergencies due to hazards, conflicts and humanitarian crises, even before the COVID-19 pandemic, which made some of the countries and territories fragile and vulnerable (2). Dengue fever, Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever (CCHF) and avian influenza continue to pose severe health risks, with high mortality rates and high economic impacts (2). Although EMR countries are improving their emergency health preparedness (EPR) through the use of tools like the International Health Regulations (IHR), significant gaps exist in the overall preparedness. The 2018 Joint External Evaluations (JEE) of IHR capacity estimates for the region range from 31/100 in Somalia to 90/100 in the UAE (3). Between 2016 and 2019, 19 countries/ territories (including the State of Palestine) developed national action plans for health security (NAPHS), which identified country priorities. However, these plans have been implemented only to a limited extent for several reasons, including the lack of political commitment, poor financing and limited human resource capacity (3). National Public Health Institutes (NPHIs) in the region, often a government agency or network of agencies that provides science-based leadership and coordination to improve health care, make substantial contributions to EPR. These are often known as Public Health Institute (PIH), National Institute of Health (NIH), National Public Health Agency (NPHA), or Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) (4). Despite the differences in the name or legal structure, all NPHIs focus on essential public health functions, offering evidence-based policy advice and health promotion (4,5). NPHI budgets range from US$ 32 920 to US$ 8.5 billion globally, depending on the country’s income level (6). In low and middle-income countries (LMICs), NPHIs often rely on financial support from international donors because government funding is often insufficient (8). There are 13 NPHIs across 11 EMR Member States, which generate research evidence for policymaking, conduct surveillance, provide field epidemiology services, manage laboratory networks, and develop health workforce (9). Seventy percent of NPHIs in the EMR function as government entities, 80% have dedicated units within the organisational structure responsible for overseeing EPR activities, and 40% have EPR plans (9). However, their role in terms of how they interlink with the wider “institutional EPR system” is not very clear (9). There are efforts to integrate NPHIs into the national emergency preparedness strategies. For example, the Regional Development and Engagement Framework for NPHIs in Emergency Preparedness and Response and the EMR Regional Committee resolution in 2022 established priorities for resilient health systems and identified key areas relevant to NPHIs. Also, a regional action plan for emergency preparedness and response outlined core NPHI actions (10). However, at t he national level, there are no detailed accounts of the functional and financial integration of NPHIs with the national EPR plans, such as the NAPHS and JEE. There is limited information on the financial support that NPHIs receive from partners. Budget information is sometimes scattered across documents, such as the national health strategies, NPHI annual plans and the NAPHS, making it scarce, inconsistent and outdated. For example, the 2019–2020 National Institute of Health Pakistan (NIH Pakistan) budget was publicly available at the time of this analysis, but it was dated and does not accurately reflect the funding needed for EPR activities, thus creating uncertainty about budget sufficiency. A recent rapid review found that 9 of 12 EMR countries/territories primarily fund NPHIs through the Ministry of Health or Ministry of Finance (11). While Gulf Cooperation Council countries like Saudi Arabia rely entirely on domestic funding, conflict-affected nations like Somalia depend solely on donor funding. Several older NPHIs, which serve as IHR focal points, including Pakistan (1980), Afghanistan (1963), Institut Pasteur du 574 Commentary EMHJ – Vol. 32 No. 9 – 2026 Maroc (IPM Morocco, 1957), Institut National d’Hygiene Morocco (INH Morocco, 1930), and Pasteur Institute of Iran (1920), receive financial support for NPHI functions in IHR technical areas, as well as allocations under NAPHS. However, the exact funding amounts remain ambiguous. For example, the latest NAPHS for Pakistan (2024–2028) shows PKR 31.44 billion over 5 years across 6 provinces (12), while Afghanistan’s NAPHS (2019–2023) estimates AFN 83.57 million for emergency response operation over 5 years (13). However, the exact role of NPHIs and the associated allocations under NAPHS remain unclear. Financing mechanisms for NPHIs that are not designated as IHR national focal points or are not fully integrated into international or national emergency preparedness frameworks are even less well defined. For example, the recent NAPHS (2019–2023) of the Saudi Public Health Authority recommends “...the Saudi CDC to ensure an all-hazard and multisectoral approach for health within the national preparedness structure... and ensure integration with other systems...”, but with unclear financial allocations for EPR functions (14). The Abu Dhabi Public Health Centre carries out emergency functions, such as improving preparedness and leading SARS-CoV-2 genomic surveillance projects. Although the recent NAPHS (2019–2023) estimates US$ 80 000 for preparedness, the responsibilities and allocations of Abu Dhabi Public Health Centre remain unclear (15). Comprehensive information on the functional and financial integration of NPHIs with national emergency preparedness plans, such as NAPHS and JEE, is needed to estimate the financial needs and financial support available to NPHIs from the government, the private sector, or development partners. We propose a strategic financing approach for NPHIs that will encourage financial sustainability, efficiency and equitable resource allocation, although sustainable financing for EPR in the region's conflict-affected countries is more challenging. We suggest the adoption of finance partnerships that combine public funds, private investments and philanthropic contributions to address uncertainty in these settings. The blended model addresses systemic inefficiencies through risk-sharing and aligning incentives with social outcomes. It supports health care infrastructure growth, expansion of access to digital health and renewable clinics, and collaboration among governments, investors and philanthropies (16). We propose three Ds: deploying domestic funding, diversifying external resources and developing contingency funds. Deploy domestic funding for emergency health preparedness Developing a clear multi-year strategy for each NPHI is essential to ensure alignment with their strategic goal and vision. Standardizing the EPR functions of NPHIs/NPHAs in accordance with global health security frameworks is crucial. The current efforts by WHO to develop EPR capabilities for NPHAs under the foundational and technical domain can be used as a reference to develop a common understanding of NPHI capabilities (17). Conducting a costing exercise will help identify the financial needs for EPR functions, and establishing a robust financial tracking system will enable robust monitoring of allocation and use of EPR funding. Defining clear roles and integrating NPHI funding into national EPR strategies and plans, alongside using monitoring tools such as JEE, SPAR and NAPHS, is needed. Lessons can be drawn from Pakistan’s NPHI, which designated the IHR focal point in 2014, with a focal person assigned to oversee the day-to-day response and reporting requirements under the IHR. NIH has been a key stakeholder in the costing for NAPHS. After the compilation of the costed 5-year plan, a final review was conducted by the technical working group for IHR NAPHS development. As the notified IHR focal point, NIH was designated to lead implementation of JEE technical areas such as surveillance and response, public health laboratory network, Emergency Operations Centre, biosafety and biosecurity, health workforce development for IHR, AMR, etc. (12). Diversify external resources for emergency health preparedness External support is an important source of funding for NPHIs. NPHIs receive partial or complete support from a range of external sources, including multilateral organisations like the World Bank, WHO, Food and Agriculture Organization, and UNICEF, followed by bilateral agencies. During the COVID-19 pandemic, most LMICs requested support from the World Bank and Pandemic Fund. Clarifying roles and responsibilities for NPHIs in EPR external financial mechanisms will strengthen existing and create new opportunities for their financial sustainability. It will enable technical and financial integration of NPHIs with other national and international actors supporting EPR efforts (18). Establishing or strengthening coordination between NPHIs, the International Association of National Public Health Institutes (IANPHI) and NPHIs of other high- income countries can support NPHIs to undertake EPR functions. IANPHI offers short-term assistance to help countries to quickly address gaps in NPHI capability and capacity, and medium-term assistance of up to US$ 50 000 annually for 3 years for priority projects in low- resource countries (4). Several NPHIs were established with assistance from a European country and often in collaboration with the NPHIs of those countries. For example, The Public Health Agency of Sweden provided financial and capacity building assistance to Somalia NIH for 6 years (2019–2025) (19). Such partnerships can play a vital role in transitioning NPHIs to financial sustainability. 575 Commentary EMHJ – Vol. 32 No. 9 – 2026 Establish dedicated contingency funds for emergency health preparedness Contingency funds serve as a crucial and efficient pillar for NPHIs to access financial resources promptly, enabling them to carry out EPR functions effectively. During COVID-19, several countries used existing or new disaster financing initiatives to support EPR. Establishing a dedicated and flexible EPR contingency fund within the Ministry of Health and/or the Ministry of Disaster Management will enable rapid allocation of EPR financial resources and streamline EPR efforts of NPHIs. One such contingency fund, known as the Revolving Outbreak Investigation Fund (ROIF), was established through a partnership between the Nigeria Center for Disease Control (NCDC), the African Field Epidemiology Network (AFENET) and Resolve to Save Lives, to create pooled and rapidly accessible funding from multiple donors for qualifying outbreak investigations (20). Funding: None. Competing interests: None declared. Three Ds for improving financial capacities of NPHIs in EMR 1. Deploy domestic funding Action 1.1: Develop a clear multi-year strategy for each NPHI, ensuring alignment with its strategic goals and vision. Action 1.2: Standardize the EPR functions of NPHIs/NPHAs in accordance with global health security frameworks and domains. Action 1.3: Conduct a costing exercise to identify the financial needs for EPR functions, and establish a robust financial tracking system to track financial allocations and use of EPR funding. Action 1.4: Establish clear roles and integrate NPHIs funding allocation into national EPR strategies and plans, including IHR monitoring tools such as JEE, SPAR and NAPHS. 2. Diversify external resources for EPR Action 2.1: Clearly define the roles of NPHIs in externally funded EPR initiatives. Provide training for NPHIs to help them independently seek dedicated funding from donor-supported EPR projects. Action 2.2: Establish or strengthen coordination between NPHIs and The International Association of National Public Health Institutes for EPR functions. Action 2.3: Establish or strengthen strategic partnerships between NPHIs and NPHIs of other high- income countries to facilitate lessons-sharing and collaborative efforts for resource generation, for EPR. 3. Establish dedicated contingency funds for EPR Action 3.1: Create or modify dedicated national and sub-national emergency contingency funds within the Ministry of Health and/or the Ministry of Disaster Management, and establish clear channels for NPHIs to use these funds. 576 Commentary EMHJ – Vol. 32 No. 9 – 2026 References 1. Volume 32, Number 11—November 2026 Dispatch Differentiating Avian and Seasonal Influenza Viruses in Wastewater by Digital PCR Suggested citation for this article Abstract Highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5Nx) viruses, particularly clade 2.3.4.4b, pose substantial global health risks. We combined and piloted 2 duplex reverse transcription digital PCRs to discriminate between avian and seasonal influenza viruses in wastewater. This approach enabled rapid, strain-specific detection to reduce ambiguity in environmental surveillance for influenza viruses. Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) A(H5Nx) viruses, particularly clade 2.3.4.4b, continue to circulate widely among wild and domestic birds, with recurrent spillover into mammalian species and sporadic infections in humans. The extensive geographic distribution and persistent circulation of clade 2.3.4.4b, together with its predominance among HPAI A(H5) viruses currently circulating in Europe, support its continued relevance for animal and public health surveillance (1–4). Wastewater and environmental surveillance (WES) provides a population-level complement to clinical, veterinary, and wildlife surveillance and is increasingly integrated into the monitoring framework in Europe (5). WES has been widely used for SARS-CoV-2 and has also been applied to influenza A and B viruses (6,7). WES typically relies on PCR-based methods to detect and quantify pathogens. Similar to other pathogens, influenza RNA concentrations in wastewater might vary according to shedding patterns, sewer inputs, matrix characteristics, and the relative contributions of human and animal sources (6). Differences in laboratory methods and reporting further complicates interpretation, underscoring the necessity of considering assay sensitivity and specificity when comparing results across studies (8). The matrix gene is the preferred molecular target for the screening of influenza A viruses (9) because it is conserved across seasonal human and animal influenza strains, but broad reactivity limits strain discrimination in mixed environmental samples. For instance, the influenza A component of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) influenza SARS-CoV-2 (Flu SC2) multiplex assay, developed for clinical respiratory specimens and real-time PCR (10) and adapted for reverse transcription digital PCR (RT-dPCR) analysis of wastewater (11), can detect both seasonal human and avian influenza A signals (12). Several wastewater assays were designed to detect H5 viruses (13–15). Those assays are useful for broad H5 virus screening but might require further characterization to distinguish between HPAI H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b, another H5 lineage, or low pathogenicity avian influenza. A clade-specific assay can provide additional epidemiologic resolution and help prioritize follow-up across animal and human surveillance. We previously developed the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre (JRC) RT-PCRs targeting the hemagglutinin (HA) and matrix protein (MP) genes. The JRC-HA assay targets a conserved HA region in HPAI H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b and the JRC-MP assay targets the conserved matrix gene for broader detection of influenza A (12) (Appendix). We evaluated a dual-duplex RT-dPCR approach combining the CDC influenza A and B assay components with the JRC-HA and JRC-MP assay to discriminate between avian and seasonal human influenza viruses in wastewater. We first performed a comparative in silico analysis of the publicly available primer and probe sequences from 3 H5 assays (13–15), and the JRC-HA and JRC-MP assays (12) (Figure 1). The predicted detection of HPAI H5 clade 2.3.4.4b was broadly comparable across the assays, but the JRC-HA assay revealed greater discrimination against non-2.3.4.4b HPAI clades (Figure 1, panel A). The JRC-HA and JRC-MP assays had the lowest predicted cross-reactivity with low pathogenicity avian influenza H5 annotated sequences (Figure 1, panels A, B). Then, we evaluated the JRC-HA and JRC-MP duplex assay by using HPAI H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b viruses collected from wild birds and poultry in northern Italy during October–December 2025 (Appendix). Sequence alignment revealed high conservation across the primer and probe binding regions for both assays, indicating that recent viral evolution had not substantially affected assay inclusivity. Nevertheless, we identified 2 substitutions within the JRC-HA probe-binding region in 3 samples (Appendix Figure 1). In silico PCR predicted amplification (data not shown), and both quantitative reverse transcription PCR and RT-dPCR detected influenza A in all 10 samples, including samples with low viral concentrations (Figure 2, panels A, B). For samples H, I, and J, lowering the JRC-HA RT-dPCR annealing temperature from 60°C to 56.4°C improved partition separation (Appendix Figure 2). At the revised annealing temperature, in silico analysis indicated that stable primer-dimer formation was unlikely, and assay specificity was not affected (Figure 2, panels C–F). The limit of detection was 5 copies/reaction, consistent with previous results (12). The CDC influenza B assay failed to detect the target in any of the 10 samples analyzed, whereas the CDC influenza A assay detected the target in all 10 samples with comparable performance to that of the JRC-HA and JRC-MP assays (Figure 2, panels A, B). Such broad detection is useful for confirming the presence of influenza virus; however, it does not permit discrimination between avian and seasonal human influenza A viruses in mixed specimens such as wastewater samples collected during periods of seasonal influenza circulation. To improve discrimination between avian and seasonal human influenza in wastewater samples, we evaluated the influenza A and B components of the CDC Flu SC2 multiplex assay together with the JRC-HA and JRC-MP duplex assay. We performed the 2 duplex assays separately, according to the conditions described previously (12) (Appendix). Because HPAI H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b–positive wastewater samples were unavailable, we added defined amounts of avian and seasonal human influenza A RNA to RNA extracts from influenza-negative wastewater samples (Figure 3). We evaluated the 2 duplex assays under 3 simulated co-circulation scenarios. In the first scenario, we added only HPAI H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b RNA to the wastewater samples. The JRC-HA, JRC-MP, and CDC influenza A assays produced comparable viral RNA copy numbers, indicating detection near the analytical limits of the JRC assays (Figure 3, panel A). For the second scenario, we combined low concentrations (10 or 20 copies/μL) of HPAI H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b RNA and seasonal influenza A RNA (35 copies/μL) to simulate periods of low seasonal influenza activity or low avian influenza prevalence. The JRC-HA and JRC-MP assays selectively detected HPAI H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b RNA, whereas the CDC influenza A assay detected both avian and seasonal human influenza A RNA without distinction (Figure 3, panel B). In the third scenario, we added low concentrations (10 or 20 copies/μL) of HPAI H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b RNA to a high concentration (3,500 copies/μL) of seasonal influenza A background, representing a possible early stage of HPAI detection during peak seasonal influenza activity. The JRC-HA assay detected HPAI H5N1 RNA without cross-reactivity, whereas the JRC-MP detected both avian and seasonal human influenza A RNA, but yielded lower copy number estimates than the CDC influenza A assay (Figure 3, panel C). Together, our results suggest that JRC-HA identifies and discriminates HPAI H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b, whereas JRC-MP provided complementary detection but might lack specificity during high seasonal influenza A circulation. We propose the complementary use of CDC Flu SC2 and JRC-HA and JRC-MP duplex assays in a dual-duplex approach (Figure 4). The influenza A and B components of the CDC Flu SC2 multiplex assay are useful for routine communitywide surveillance of influenza A and B, ensuring continuity of the current public health reporting system. The JRC-HA and JRC-MP duplex assay, after the CDC Flu SC2 duplex, is used to specifically identify the occurrence of HPAI H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b virus in a population, providing an early-warning capability that is effective in the presence of seasonal influenza backgrounds. We evaluated our dual duplex RT-dPCR by using animal-derived viral material and spiked wastewater RNA extracts, rather than confirmed HPAI-positive wastewater samples. Further field evaluation will be useful to assess performance under naturally occurring conditions and in different wastewater matrices. Because influenza viruses evolve rapidly, periodic sequence-based evaluations, followed by experimental validation and assay updates when necessary, will be required to maintain assay performance as new H5 clades emerge. A clade-specific wastewater result would not by itself determine a different public health response from a broad H5-positive result. However, it could reduce ambiguity, prioritize confirmatory testing, and enable integration of wastewater findings with veterinary, wildlife, domestic animal, and human surveillance data. Dr. Paracchini is employed as scientific officer at the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre in Geel, Belgium. Her research interests include working on the development of novel assays and reference materials for enhanced pathogen surveillance such as SARS-CoV-2, avian influenza, and antimicrobial resistance.
